concept.name: Inverted yield curve
concept.definition: A yield curve configuration in which shorter-maturity yields exceed longer-maturity yields, giving the curve a downward slope. The U.S. Treasury notes that short-term rates can exceed longer-term rates when market expectations about future rates and monetary policy shift; inversions have historically preceded U.S. recessions, though the relationship is a statistical regularity, not a causal law.
concept.intuition: Investors accept lower yields on long bonds because they expect rates to fall in the future — often because they expect the central bank to cut rates in a slowdown.
concept.mechanics: Measured as a negative term spread, e.g. the 10-year Treasury constant maturity yield minus the 2-year (FRED series T10Y2Y) falling below zero. Inversions often arise when policy tightening pushes short rates up while long yields stay anchored by weak growth expectations.
concept.formula: Inversion when y(short) − y(long) > 0, e.g. 2-year CMT − 10-year CMT > 0.
concept.failure_modes: Inversions have produced false or very early recession signals, and post-2008 term premium compression (e.g. from quantitative easing) can invert curves without implying a downturn; timing between inversion and recession varies widely.
concept.misconceptions: Inversion does not cause recessions, nor does it guarantee one; it is an indicator of market expectations and term premia, not a mechanical trigger.
concept.example: In 2022–2023 the 2-year Treasury yield rose above the 10-year yield, leaving the 2s10s spread negative for an extended period.

citations.source: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Interest Rates — Frequently Asked Questions
citations.section: Why do longer CMT maturities sometimes have yields lower than the shorter maturities (i.e., "inverted yield curve rates")?

citations.source: FRED, 10-Year Treasury Constant Maturity Minus 2-Year Treasury Constant Maturity [T10Y2Y]
